accroche: In April 1902, Teisserenc de Bort announces that the air stops cooling above 8 to 12 km. Three days later, Assmann announces the same thing in Berlin.
contenu_vulgarise:
At the start of the 20th century, one rule seems self-evident: the higher you go, the colder it gets. It had been measured on mountains and in the first balloons; it was extended, without measurement, to the upper layers of the atmosphere.

Léon Teisserenc de Bort put it to the test. His tool was the sounding balloon: a balloon with no passenger, carrying a recording thermometer and barometer, which climbs until it bursts, then lets the instrument fall back, to be found and its trace read.

## A Measurement Set Aside

As early as November 1896, one of his balloons reached 14 kilometers. The temperature there stopped falling between about 12 and 14 kilometers. This result was set aside as a measurement error: it contradicted what was expected, and people preferred to extend the expected curve upward.

Teisserenc de Bort did not defend it with an argument, but with numbers. He multiplied his ascents, under varied conditions, notably at night, so that the Sun's radiation could not be blamed for distorting the thermometer. According to Birner, it took him nearly ten years before he dared announce the result. The sources do not agree on the count: more than two hundred soundings collected according to Birner's page in Munich, twenty-five soundings near Paris for the announcement according to the SCMO Bulletin.

## Two Announcements in Three Days

On April 28, 1902, he announced to the French Academy of Sciences the existence of an “isothermal zone”: from 8 to 12 kilometers depending on the case, temperature stops falling with altitude.

Three days later, Richard Assmann made the same announcement to the German academy, from Berlin. He had taken the opposite route: few soundings, six in his report, but instruments he had painstakingly improved. He spoke of an “upper inversion.”

The two men reached the same result by opposite routes: one through a large number of soundings, the other through care. That is what gives the episode its force: two opposite methods do not go wrong in the same way.

## A Name for the Layer Above

Around 1908, Teisserenc de Bort proposed a name for the case: the lower layer, where the air churns, is the troposphere; the one above, where the layers are seen stacking up, the stratosphere.

What changes, once this is understood, is the nature of the rule we thought we knew. Cooling with altitude is true, but only up to a certain height. And that height varies: Teisserenc de Bort already noted that it is lower during cyclones (low-pressure systems) and higher during anticyclones.

The first measurement that contradicted the rule had been filed among the errors. We do not know how many others are still waiting in that category.

repere.texte: On April 28, 1902, Teisserenc de Bort announces to the French Academy of Sciences an “isothermal zone” after a large number of soundings made under varied conditions, at night in particular; three days later, Assmann announces a similar result to the German academy, drawn from six soundings.
repere.source: Thomas Birner, “Richard Assmann and the Discovery of the Stratosphere,” American Meteorological Society, 95th Annual Meeting, 2015

carte.punch: Above 8 to 12 km, temperature stops falling. At first it was thought to be an error.
carte.idee: Until 1902, it was believed that air always cools as it rises. Teisserenc de Bort, through a large number of soundings, and Assmann, through six careful soundings, show that the decline stops: this is the stratosphere.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Birner: Richard Assmann and the Discovery of the Stratosphere

quiz.question: Why were the first isothermal readings set aside at first?
choix: Because the balloons carried no thermometer at that height
Because continuous cooling was expected and it was seen as a measurement error
Because the balloons burst before reaching 8 kilometers
Because only Assmann had instruments precise enough
quiz.explication: It was assumed that the decline observed near the ground continued higher up, and a result that contradicted it passed for an error. Teisserenc de Bort's balloon had nonetheless reached 14 kilometers as early as November 1896; it took nearly ten years of soundings before he dared announce the result.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What makes the agreement between Teisserenc de Bort and Assmann so convincing?
choix: They reached the same result by opposite methods
Assmann had taken over Teisserenc de Bort's balloons and instruments
The two academies had decided in advance to confirm the result
Their measurements were taken in the same place, on the same day
quiz_supplementaire.explication: One multiplied the soundings, the other perfected the instruments (six soundings). The two announcements, in Paris and in Berlin, are separated by only three days.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Teisserenc de Bort already note about the height at which temperature stops falling?
choix: It is the same everywhere and in every season
It is higher during cyclones than during anticyclones
It is lower during cyclones, higher during anticyclones
It is lower at night than during the day
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that this height varies: lower during cyclones (low-pressure systems), higher during anticyclones. The cooling rule therefore holds only up to a changing height.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Teisserenc de Bort launch balloons at night in particular?
choix: Because the instruments do not work in broad daylight
So that the Sun's radiation does not distort the thermometer
To keep the balloons from bursting earlier in the heat
quiz_supplementaire.explication: He wants to rule out the objection that the Sun heats the thermometer. He defends his result through the number of soundings, under varied conditions, night included.
